The same provenance principle is extended to communications with academic units concerning quotation, citation, attribution, and permission to reuse research material. Such communications are treated as research-provenance events because they document how research material moves between researchers, institutions, academic audiences, and subsequent publications. The methodological cycle remains: OBSERVE → RECORD → VERIFY → PRESERVE → COMPARE → RESPOND → LEARN Version 7 therefore expands the original observation model into the following research-evidence pathway: Institutional Communication → Observation → Evidence → Research Provenance → Open Research Output → Longitudinal Analysis → Learning The framework establishes explicit boundaries between: acknowledgement and substantive review; permission and endorsement; public-record pathways and confirmed publication; temporal sequence and causal evidence; institutional communication and institutional adoption; research dissemination and institutional validation. This bounded-inference approach enables institutional interactions to be studied without converting administrative communication into unsupported conclusions. Version 7 further connects OBSERVE with emerging AI Accountability Literacy, particularly the methodological questions of how AI actions can be identified, authenticated, authorized, observed, recorded, verified, and preserved as research evidence. The framework is designed for research involving digital platforms, public and private institutions, regulatory environments, AI systems, agentic AI, citizen auditing, institutional observation, research provenance, open science, and longitudinal accountability research. Its central methodological proposition is: When institutional accountability increasingly depends upon traceable evidence, the provenance, verification, preservation, and longitudinal comparability of institutional observation become part of the research infrastructure through which accountability can be studied. OBSERVE Protocol v1.0 — Version 7 is therefore not a legal framework, regulatory assessment, judicial determination, or institutional evaluation. It is a research and evidence infrastructure designed to make institutional observation reproducible, auditable, provenance-aware, and suitable for longitudinal research. Version 7 treats the research record as cumulative. Earlier observations are not overwritten by later developments. New institutional communications, responses, permissions, public records, publications, technical changes, non-responses, and other observable events are added as subsequent research events. The record remains open to verification, comparison, and learning. items.title: Occupational Hazards and Utilization of Personal Protective Devices Among Motorcycle Riders in Rivers West Senatorial District, Rivers State, Nigeria
items.abstract: Motorcycle riders face numerous occupational risks as a result of their exposure to road traffic accidents, environmental conditions, and ergonomic difficulties. This study looked at the use of personal protective equipment and occupational hazards by motorcycle riders in Rivers West Senatorial District, Rivers State. Five objectives, five research questions, and two hypotheses were developed and tested to a significance level of 0.05. With a population of 8,595 motorcyclists in Rivers West Senatorial District, Rivers State, and a sample size of 756 motorcyclists from Rivers West's various local governments, the study employed a descriptive cross-sectional survey design. The reliability coefficient of the self-structured questionnaire that was used for data collection was 0.91, and it was validated by three professors in the department of Human Kinetics, Health, and Safety Education. According to the study's findings, the result demonstrated that motorcyclists were particularly susceptible to physical danger (3.06 0.48). The findings of this study are to be expected because riders are exposed to numerous physically hazardous factors while riding. There was a negative correlation because when riders use personal protective devices like nose masks, eye goggles, and protective clothing, they are less likely to be exposed to physical hazards. When riders use PPD, they are more likely to be exposed to more hazards. It was recommended among others that management of road transport workers should put necessary laws to enforce the utilization of personal protective devices like eye goggle, nose masks, reflective and helmet by drivers or riders to reduce exposure to physical hazards and accidents among motorcyclists, the national union of road transport workers NURTW through their various bodies in rural and urban areas should establish regulatory personnel’s to ensure that there is strict compliance to safety by putting on the necessary protective devices by drivers/riders and fine should be paid for those that fail to comply.

items.title: Occupational Health Risks and Socioeconomic Dimensions of Solid Waste Scavenging in Potiskum Metropolis, Yobe State, Nigeria
items.abstract: Solid waste scavenging provides livelihood for many in Nigeria but exposes scavengers to health hazards and chronic diseases. This study assessed solid waste scavenging and its potential health risks in Potiskum Metropolis, Yobe State. Using a descriptive survey design, 386 respondents were sampled from five wards. Data were collected through simple random and accidental sampling at dumpsites and analyzed using descriptive statistics. Findings revealed that most scavengers were male (97%), largely under 18 years (62%), and earned daily income above ₦950 (42%). Use of personal protective equipment (PPE) was low. Major health problems included infectious diseases, respiratory problems, injury, fatigue, and skin infections. Recommendations include PPE promotion, skill acquisition programs, formalization and monitoring of scavenging activities, and health awareness campaigns

items.title: Old Ideas, Novel Problems: The Instability of LLM-Based Novelty Evaluation
items.abstract: Automated ideation systems are often evaluated on the novelty of the ideas they produce, and that judgment is increasingly delegated to large language models. Such judges are typically built ad hoc and validated, if at all, on human-authored papers rather than on the generated ideas they are meant to score. So, how do novelty judges perform? Not well. We present a systematic controlled study of novelty evaluation design choices. We first build an evaluation set automatically, mining OpenReview for passages where reviewers explicitly affirm or dispute a paper's originality and keeping only submissions with unanimous agreement at the extremes of their research area; we pair these with ideas from a vanilla LLM generator. Across six judges, we find that small prompt design choices have large consequences; e.g., simply telling the judge that reviewers found one idea novel and the other not can change its verdict on more than half of the identical idea pairs it is shown, shifting pairwise accuracy by over 50 points and occasionally pushing it below chance. The same change helps one judge and hurts another. Retrieval and larger reasoning budgets help little, and two purpose-built novelty evaluators are outperformed by our cheapest prompted baseline. These results raise questions about reported novelty gains of automated ideation systems, and call for robust novelty evaluation methods.
